Before we can install Sonarqube in the SSW DMZ, we need to have a fully defined installation procedure. This will allow us to save massive time during the actual install and prevent encountering any major roadblocks or unexpected behaviors.

 

The expected output is a confluence article walking through the install procedure at a command-by-command level.

The best way to do this would probably be to setup a VM and run the actual install there as a prototype, documenting along the way. I expect this to roughly follow or be very close to the already existing Sonarqube installation procedure that Sonarqube will provide on their website. We just want to modify it for our environment and try to ensure it's written around automating as much as possible.

On Friday I was able to get the idm to redirect using the nginx server I created. The actual URL is a little different than what I had identified in a previous comment above. All web apps will look similar to the IDM url which is idm.cwsdeveng.com . So, new URL's will have the name of the app at the beinging of the URL. 

in order to use a vanity URL like the idm.cwsdeveng.com you will need to add the URL name to the principal name so the name is associated with the certificate. You can add that using the following example: ipa service-add-principal HTTP/:ssw-phc-s7-vm-idm.cwsdeveng.com HTTP:/idm.cwsdeveng.com so you list the actual Pincipal Name which is the FQDN of the server, followed by the vanity URL you wish to use. Once that is updated you can successfully create the certificates with the vanity URL that will live on the websever, and add an aliase entry into DNS so the new name. There is more to it than that, but at high level once this is completed you will be able to access the new URL.

column33:
Install / implement TANG & CLEVIS on ssw-phc-s9

Overview:
Clevis: A pluggable, client-side decryption framework that runs on the machine with encrypted storage. It integrates with LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup) to unlock drives.
Tang: A server that stores cryptographic keys and provides them to clients, but only when they are on the same secure network. It is stateless and does not require databases or TLS certificates.
How They Work Together: When a machine boots, Clevis requests the decryption key from the Tang server. If the network connection is successful, the disk is unlocked automatically. If the server is unreachable (e.g., the machine is stolen), the disk remains locked.
Security Advantages: This approach secures data at rest while providing automated, secure booting for servers in data centers or remote locations, avoiding the need for human intervention.

*SUSPENSE: FRIDAY, 09 JANUARY 2026*

Good afternoon,

Please review hardware lists for GlobalFoundaries Fab 8 (Malta, NY) Technologies and provide an equity or no equity response to PMS 394 Cyber (CC Line) by EOD Friday, 09 January 2026.  

From the tasker below, disregard the instructions to fill out a form and disregard the 12/30/2025 suspense date.

//

Regarding Tasker: CATMS-191225-M2PP | Loss of Access to GlobalFoundries Fab 8 (Malta, NY) Technologies Effective 31 Mar 2026

Action ID: USA002679-25 | Action Request Type: Coordination Request

Tasker Response Type: FAA-For Appropriate Action | CATMS Tasker Role: OCR

Subject: Loss of Access to GlobalFoundries Fab 8 (Malta, NY) Technologies Effective 31 Mar 2026 

Due to recent government budget reallocations, effective 31 Mar 2026, the Trusted Access Program Office (TAPO) may lose access to semiconductor technologies (chips) at GlobalFoundries Fab 8 in Malta, NY.  

GlobalFoundries Fab 8 is the sole domestic source for multiple advanced process nodes (e.g., 12nm, 22nm, 45nm). These technologies are integral to the production and sustainment of critical systems across all warfighting domains.

TAPO needs to inform the Department of War (DoW) of the scope of potential impacts to DoW systems.

 

Chips from GlobalFoundries support: 
 * Satellite and secure communications
 * Advanced radar and sensor systems
 * Missile guidance and control systems
 * Next-generation computing for AI and electronic warfare
 * Radiation hardened applications 
 * Smart Munitions & Guidance
 * Classified Manufacturing 

To ensure we can continue to meet the Department’s access requirements effectively, we are requesting information regarding your manufacturing requirements at the GlobalFoundries Fab 8 facility. 

TAPO is requesting data relevant to your future manufacturing requirements at Malta, utilizing any of the following technologies, for FY26 through FY31:
 * 12LP (12nm)
 * 12LP+ (12nm)
 * 22FDX (22nm)
 * 45RFSOI (45nm)
 * 45SPCLO (45nm)
 * 12SOI (45nm)
 * Advanced Packaging (2.5D/3D) 

 

Please fill out the attached form, so your requirements are accurately communicated to Headquarters. Near-term funding decisions will directly determine the future availability of these resources.   Please supply the requested information by 12/30/2025. If no response is received, TAPO will assume that your organization no longer requires manufacturing capabilities at GlobalFoundries Fab 8, Malta, NY.

In LM-Gov't-EB Cyber tag-up on 12/18/25, we had a discussion about the PTRs for the SSLR resulting from the windows NAVSEA letter from Oct 2024. The discussion said that Open Source SW isn't required; COTs can be used, but all SW needs approval from NAVSEA. Pat Turner had me send him the requirements so he can discuss with NAVSEA.

He sent me back this email. Upon looking at the PSS and SLR, there are not requirements or PTRs to invoke the Cyber spec:

---------------------

Thank you for bringing this up. As a result of this discussion, I reviewed the Windows letter and noted EB actions in section 5, and an LM action in section 6 that have not been tracked. Your proposed requirements are a great start however apply to the PSS. I am opening a conversation with PMS-394 as we continue to develop in formal documentation to determine the best place for these requirements. I also need to understand whether the PSS will reference the cyber spec and if so, should any requirements be moved out of the PSS, as we are doing for the SLR.

I will let you know how this evolves.

-----------------------

My response:

Pat,

 

I did a little research on my end in regards to the Cyber Spec being invoked in SLR and PSS requirements. I know that the Platform Systems Engineering group authoring those documents just received the final NAVSEA feedback from Sigmund Young that EB will be incorporating into the documents. Many changes were in response to the comment to change any reference to “applicable contract” to “Cybersecurity Specification 25-MES-050597”. The only change that I see is for SSW-PSS-528:

 

(U) Developmental and Operational Security – PHC development, integration, and operations shall be conducted in accordance with the Cybersecurity Specification 25-MES-050597, security classification guidance, and regulations (e.g. DoDI 8500.01 Cybersecurity).

 

This appears to be the only place where the Cyber Spec will be invoked in the PSS, and I do not see an instance of it being invoked in the SLR. I know there were comments on the cyber document tree to invoke the Cyber Spec in the SLR, PSS, and all SSLRs via a new requirement. I will discuss this with folks on the EB end because I do not know that there are currently any PTRs to add requirements invoking the Cyber Spec.

And one thing to clarify in my email below, the Windows and OSS requirements are being added to the SLR and the SSLRs. I was incorrect in putting the [SSW-PSS-##] numbering since it is not being added in the PSS.

 

Please let me know how I can facilitate some of the required changes. We can sync-up in the new year.

Currently the D454 Network segment has dual-homed devices (Server 9, & SSW servers) which are connected to the CWS switch and local network. The concern is that the nature of these dual homed and dual managed systems creates a route for unauthorized devices to have access to the greater UIS008 network.  This route would allow a method of infiltration and exfiltration of data, as well as an increased attack surface to at least one of the primary source code repositories on UIS008. 

This task creates a POAM for reducing the number of dual-homed devices & applying firewall rules that remediate the concerns.

Background:
 * D454 SSW-PHC has a request for D448 CWS Network Engineering (D448) to enable a feature within a UIS008/CWS hosted Gitlab referred to as "Container Registry". 

 * The container registry was enabled on both UIS008/CWS hosted Gitlab instances.

 * To date, SSW-PHC is already running a container registry on one the requested systems. 

 * SSW-PHC is planning to utilize the same server and registry to mirror the contents of the primary container registry hosted on UIS008 managed by D448.  In doing so, this gives them the ability to provide a container registry (mirrored from the UIS008 D448 managed primary registry), that is available from systems within their segment.  Systems within that segment are managed at least in part by SSW-PHC Cyber. 

Current concerns from D448:
 * Concerns around the network architecture and data flow within the segment.

I have researched the Arista platform to automate with scripts.

Findings: A script can be created to run the EOS commands required to validate each STIG vulnerability. It will make use of EOS commands and bash scripting. I can be set to run periodically on the switch. The script will create a CKL file that can then be copied to the networks library of executed STIGs for each device. The base STIG CKL file will be used as the input template that the script will modify as a "Here" document as per Bash scripting. This uses variable tags in the Here Doc. The variables will get expanded with content from the details of the Arista switch being STIGed and the commands that were run to test the vulnerability plus the output and the analysis of the output for each vulnerability. This script will also set the FINDING/NOFINDING based on the analysis of the output data for each item. 

This script can be initiated via local switch scheduling or by Ansible.  The Ansible solution will require installation of automation libraries.  Ansible will use the script to "run" the STIG check but will also collect the resultant file and place it in Cybers library of STIG runs.

The STIGs have been run manually by [~jcabral7]  with numerous findings. We will not be able to effectively make the changes required based on those finding until we configure a test network with an Arista switch and at least one server host for testing the changes before we apply them to the active SSW PHC environment. Additionally the switches are NOT up to date with the latest EOS updates, one and half years out. Last EOS version is from July of 2024.

We are currently running a basic firewall on each server with a list of ports,protocols that we use in the bldg 30 lab. However despite having a firewall it is not STIG compliant. We need to create a firewall with multiple zones to include a drop zone. Related STIGs are as follows:

RHEL-09-251010: RHEL 9 must have the firewalld package installed. 
RHEL-09-251015: The firewalld service on RHEL 9 must be active. 
RHEL-09-251020: A RHEL 9 firewall must employ a deny-all, allow-by-exception policy for allowing connections to other systems. This involves setting the default zone to drop and then adding exceptions as needed. 
RHEL-09-251025: RHEL 9 must control remote access methods. 
Other related STIGs
V-270180: The RHEL 9 fapolicy module must be configured to use a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy for software programs, as described in stigviewer.com. 
V-257935: This finding is related to the STIG rule RHEL-09-251010, requiring the firewalld package to be installed.
